questions.prompt: Which one of the following process state transitions is NOT possible?
questions.explanation: A blocked process whose I/O completes moves to Ready, not straight to Running — it must still be selected by the scheduler. The other three transitions correspond to preemption, dispatch and I/O completion.

questions.prompt: Dispatch latency is best defined as:

options.text: The total time a process spends waiting in the ready queue
The time an I/O operation takes to complete
The time between submitting a job and its completion
The time to stop one process and start another running

questions.explanation: Dispatch latency is the overhead the dispatcher incurs switching context, switching to user mode, and jumping to the right instruction. It is pure overhead and matters most in real-time systems.

questions.prompt: A running process issues an I/O request. What state does it move to?
questions.explanation: The process cannot proceed until the I/O completes, so it leaves the CPU and waits in the blocked state. It returns to Ready once the device signals completion.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following need NOT be saved when the operating system switches context from one process to another?

options.text: Contents of the translation lookaside buffer

questions.explanation: The TLB is a cache of translations, not architectural state — it is simply flushed (or tagged with an address space id) on a switch. Registers, PC and PSW must all be preserved to resume the process correctly.

questions.prompt: What is swap space on disk used for?

options.text: Storing pages evicted from physical memory

questions.explanation: Swap space backs virtual memory: when physical frames run short, pages are written out to swap and read back on demand. It is what allows a process's address space to exceed RAM.

questions.prompt: In a system with n CPUs, what is the maximum number of processes that can be in the Ready state?
questions.explanation: The Ready queue holds every runnable process not currently executing, and its length is bounded only by how many processes exist. It is the Running state that is capped at n.

questions.prompt: Under preemptive scheduling, which of the following transitions can occur?

options.text: Ready to Blocked, caused by a timer interrupt
Blocked to Running, caused by I/O completion
Terminated to Ready, caused by a restart
Running to Ready, caused by the scheduler

questions.explanation: Preemption is exactly the Running to Ready transition — the scheduler takes the CPU away from a process that could still run. A ready process is not waiting on anything, so it cannot become blocked.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following does NOT interrupt a running process?
questions.explanation: The scheduler is not an independently running process that can seize the CPU; it executes as part of the kernel while handling some other interrupt or trap. The other three are genuine asynchronous events.

options.text: Compiling several programs into one binary
Executing one program on several CPUs at once
Executing several programs concurrently by switching the CPU between them
Allowing several users to share a single terminal

questions.explanation: Multiprogramming keeps several processes in memory and switches the CPU to another whenever the current one blocks, which raises CPU utilisation. It requires no more than a single processor.

questions.prompt: The operating system prevents an already running user process from modifying other processes because:

options.text: User processes are always loaded into read-only memory
Each process runs on a dedicated processor
The compiler removes all unsafe instructions
Memory protection hardware traps accesses outside the process's address space

questions.explanation: Isolation is enforced at runtime by the MMU: an address outside the process's mapped region raises a fault. Compile-time checks cannot help, since a process can compute addresses at runtime.
